1181.event_title: Eva Nansen at home while the Fram drifts through the Arctic
1181.event: The singer Eva Sars married the polar explorer Fridtjof Nansen on 6 September 1889, and he was often away on expeditions. In June 1893 Nansen sailed north on the Fram, which was frozen into the Arctic ice and drifted for about three years before returning to Christiania in September 1896. During his absences Eva continued to sing at concerts and kept a warm home for the family.
1181.explanation: Eva Nansen's life shows the long, quiet side of a famous expedition: the spouse who stays behind for years while the journey goes on.
1181.tie_back: The kural's wife says she herself let her husband go and so has no one else to blame for her pining, and Eva Nansen lived through three years of a separation that came with marrying an explorer.
1181._accuracy_note: Next-best: a wife at home through a long chosen separation fits the setting, but the sources do not record her explicitly consenting to the voyage or describe her grief.

1182.event_title: Ramesses II honours Queen Nefertari in temple and tomb
1182.place: Abu Simbel and the Valley of the Queens, Egypt
1182.event: Nefertari was the first wife and favourite queen of the pharaoh Ramesses II. Ramesses had her likeness carved on temple walls and statues long after he had taken other wives, and at Abu Simbel a temple was dedicated to the goddess Hathor and to Nefertari. Her tomb in the Valley of the Queens was decorated with paintings regarded as masterpieces of the age.
1182.explanation: Nefertari's monuments show a queen whose standing came from the honour her husband publicly gave her.
1182.tie_back: In the kural the pallor spreads proudly over the wife's body because 'he gave it', and Nefertari's image was spread across Egypt's monuments with the pride of something her husband had bestowed.
1182._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the pride of bearing something the beloved gave is a loose parallel, but honour is the opposite of the kural's pallor of grief; the Britannica support for the Abu Simbel temple is a photo caption.

1183.event_title: Sappho describes the bodily symptoms of love
1183.event: The Greek lyric poet Sappho of Lesbos (c. 620-570 BCE) wrote a famous poem, often numbered fragment 31, in which the speaker watches the person she loves sitting with someone else. The poem lists what love does to her body: her voice fails, a thin fire runs under her skin, her ears roar, she sweats and trembles, and she turns the colour of dried grass. Only about 650 lines of Sappho's poetry survive.
1183.explanation: The poem is the oldest well-known description in Western literature of love as a bodily illness that changes the lover's colour.
1183.tie_back: The kural's heroine says love took her beauty and gave her sickness and pallor in exchange, and Sappho, centuries earlier and far away, recorded the same pale, fevered body that love leaves behind.
1183._accuracy_note: Reasonable: love as a sickness that drains the lover's colour matches closely, but it is a poem rather than an outward event, and its setting is jealousy, not separation from a husband.

1184.event_title: Queen Artemisia builds the Mausoleum for King Mausolus
1184.event: Artemisia II was the sister and wife of King Mausolus of Caria, and after his death around 353 BCE she ruled alone for about three years. She built for him at Halicarnassus the great tomb called the Mausoleum, which was counted among the Seven Wonders of the World. Artemisia died before it was completed and was buried there with her husband; later the Romans called any grand tomb a mausoleum after it.
1184.explanation: Artemisia devoted her short reign to a monument that kept her husband's name before the world, which it still does in the word mausoleum.
1184.tie_back: The kural's wife says she thinks only of her husband and speaks only of his worth, and Artemisia turned her whole reign into a monument to her husband's name.
1184._accuracy_note: Next-best: devotion to the husband's memory fits, but this is mourning after death, and the kural's point (constant remembrance should have prevented the pallor) has no parallel.

1185.event_title: Ovid's last night in Rome before exile
1185.event: In 8 CE the emperor Augustus banished the poet Ovid to Tomis on the Black Sea (modern Constanta, Romania). In his Tristia, poems largely addressed to his wife, Ovid describes his last night in Rome: his wife weeping in his arms and praying at the household shrine, his own repeated delays at the threshold, and his wife clinging to him and asking to follow him into exile. When he refused and left, she collapsed in grief.
1185.explanation: Ovid's account is one of the most vivid surviving descriptions from the ancient world of the moment of parting between husband and wife.
1185.tie_back: The kural sets side by side the husband walking away and the pallor already spreading over the wife, and Ovid records his wife falling in grief at the very moment he went out of the door.
1185._accuracy_note: Strong: the instant collapse of the wife as the husband departs closely matches the kural, though the account is Ovid's own poetic description and the parting was forced, not a journey she agreed to.

1186.event_title: Martha Washington joins George at his winter camps
1186.place: Valley Forge, Morristown and other encampments, United States
1186.event: During the eight years of the American Revolutionary War, Martha Washington travelled each winter, when fighting largely paused, to join her husband at his headquarters, including Valley Forge and Morristown. Her stays often lasted several months in cramped quarters shared with his officers, and she is estimated to have spent about half the war at his side.
1186.explanation: Martha Washington chose hardship in camp rather than long separation at home whenever the war allowed it.
1186.tie_back: The kural says pallor lies in wait for the moment the husband's embrace loosens, as darkness waits for a lamp to fail, and Martha Washington went to her husband whenever she could so as not to leave that gap open longer than necessary.
1186._accuracy_note: Next-best: shortening separation fits the kural's fear of any gap, but the sources do not record her motive or any sign of pining in his absence.

1187.event_title: Ida Straus stays with her husband on the Titanic
1187.event: Isidor Straus, co-owner of Macy's department store, and his wife Ida, aged 63, were passengers on the RMS Titanic. Isidor declined a place in a lifeboat under the rule of women and children first, and Ida, who had nearly entered a lifeboat, turned back to stay with him despite friends urging her to go. Both were lost in the sinking.
1187.explanation: Ida Straus's choice became one of the most remembered acts of devotion of the disaster.
1187.tie_back: The kural's wife says that even turning aside a little from her husband's embrace let the pallor rush over her, and Ida Straus refused to be parted from her husband even for the safety of a lifeboat.
1187._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: the refusal of even a brief separation fits, but the setting is a disaster and death rather than the ordinary absences the kural describes.

1188.event_title: Catherine of Aragon refuses to accept the annulment of her marriage
1188.event: Henry VIII sought to end his marriage to Catherine of Aragon mainly because she had not given him a male heir. Archbishop Thomas Cranmer annulled the marriage on 23 May 1533, but Catherine refused to accept it and kept calling herself queen, until the 1534 Act of Succession required her to use the title Princess Dowager. She was separated from her daughter Mary, confined to residences including Kimbolton, and died there in January 1536.
1188.explanation: The official reasons for ending the marriage centred on Catherine, while it was Henry who set her aside.
1188.tie_back: The kural complains that people say 'she has grown pale' but no one says 'he has left her', and Catherine bore the official blame for a marriage that her husband chose to end.
1188._accuracy_note: Partial: blame falling on the abandoned wife fits, but Catherine's story is about a deliberate annulment, not a husband's absence, and the event has been used once elsewhere in the book in a related form.

1189.event_title: George Washington writes to Martha on taking command of the army
1189.event: On 18 June 1775 George Washington wrote to his wife Martha from Philadelphia that Congress had placed the army under his command and that he must go to Boston. He told her he had tried to avoid the post, partly because he did not want to leave his family, that his chief unhappiness would be knowing she was uneasy at being left alone, and he asked her to summon her fortitude and spend the time as agreeably as she could. In the months that followed Martha remained at home amid fears for her safety, and later joined him at his winter camps.
1189.explanation: The letter shows a husband persuading his wife to accept a separation for the sake of his duty and standing.
1189.tie_back: The kural's wife says that if the man who sweetly persuaded her to let him go is well and in good standing, her own pallor does not matter, and Washington's letter is exactly such a gentle persuasion to bear his absence for the sake of his public duty.
1189._accuracy_note: Reasonable: the husband's gentle persuasion to accept his departure matches closely, but we have his letter, not Martha's reply, so her own acceptance is inferred; Mount Vernon confirms the 1775 circumstances, while the letter's wording comes from the primary source.

1190.event_title: Eliza Hamilton spends fifty years defending her husband's memory
1190.event: In 1797 Alexander Hamilton's affair with Maria Reynolds became public, humiliating his wife Eliza. After Hamilton's death in 1804 she lived another fifty years, hired assistants to organize his papers, recruited biographers, and in 1846 petitioned Congress to fund publication of his writings, after which Congress passed legislation to publish and preserve them. She also helped found New York's first private orphanage in 1806 and died in 1854, aged 97.
1190.explanation: Despite the public humiliation his conduct had caused her, Eliza devoted the rest of her life to making sure her husband's name was remembered with honour.
1190.tie_back: The kural's wife would rather carry the name of 'the pale one' herself than have people slander the husband who was unkind to her, and Eliza Hamilton bore her own humiliation while spending decades protecting her husband's reputation.
1190._accuracy_note: Strong: shielding the husband's name despite his unkindness matches the kural's core, though Eliza's work came after his death rather than during an absence.
